symbols.name: satisfies
symbols.returns: true when version matches the range. Grammar (checked in this order): whitespace after a run of > < = is removed; a range containing '||' is split on '||' and is true when some part is (left to right, stops at the first true); else a range containing ' - ' becomes '>=A <=B' from split(' - ', 2); else a range containing an ASCII space is trimmed, runs of 2+ whitespace collapse to one space, it is split on ' ' and is true when every part is (stops at the first false); else the leading run of < > = ~ ^ is the operator ('=' when absent); '^' and '~' use the caret/tilde rules on the first three segments, any other run goes to compare().

leaks.description: The semver regex (and /^[v\d]/, and the validateStrict regex) run as ECMAScript RegExp without the u flag: \d is ASCII 0-9 only; the i flag uses non-unicode canonicalization, so K (U+212A), long s (U+017F) and dotless i (U+0131) do not match [a-z]; $ matches only at the very end (no match before a trailing \n). A Rust regex is Unicode-aware by default (\d matches Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits, (?i) folds K and long s), so each of these needs (?-u) or explicit ASCII classes.

The semver regex accepts any run of v ^ ~ < > = (and V through the i flag) before the first digit, so compareVersions('>=1.0.0', '1.0.0') is 0 and compareVersions('V1.0.0', '1.0.0') is 0. validate additionally requires the first character to be a lowercase v or a digit, so validate('v=1.0.0') and validate('vv1.0.0') are true and validate('V1.0.0') is false.

Each segment and pre-release identifier goes through parseInt(v, 10): the leading digit prefix is the value ('10a' is 10, '1-2' is 1, '0x10' is 0, '1e3' is 1), a leading '-' gives a negative number ('-5'), and only an identifier without a leading digit stays a string. So '1.0.0-10a' equals '1.0.0-10b', and '1.0.0-11' is above '1.0.0-1a' (semver says below).

Parsed numbers are IEEE-754 doubles: digit runs above 2^53 round (9007199254740993 equals 9007199254740992), runs of about 309+ digits become Infinity and equal each other. u64 or i64 parsing in Rust overflows or differs at these inputs.

When one side parses to a number and the other stays a string, both are compared as strings and the number is formatted with JS String(): -0 becomes '0', overflowed values become 'Infinity' or '-Infinity', 1e21 and above use exponent form. '1.0.0--0' is above '1.0.0--a' (the raw text '-0' would be below), and a 400-digit identifier is above 'Alpha' but below 'alpha'.
String identifiers compare with JS < and > (UTF-16 code units). The regex restricts identifiers to ASCII, so this equals byte order, but it is case-sensitive: 'Beta' < 'alpha', 'RC' < 'rc'.

'x', 'X' and '*' compare equal to anything, in numeric segments and also as a whole pre-release identifier ('1.0.0-x' equals '1.0.0-alpha'). The resulting order is not transitive: 1.x = 1.5 and 1.x = 1.7 but 1.5 < 1.7. Wildcards are not allowed in the first segment.

A missing segment or identifier counts as '0' (a[i] || '0'), not as a wildcard: '1.0.0-alpha' equals '1.0.0-alpha.0', compareVersions('1.2.3', '1.x') is 1, and satisfies('1.2.3', '1.x') is false while satisfies('1.2.0', '1.x') is true.

Pre-release precedence reuses compareSegments: numeric against alphanumeric follows parseInt and string order, not semver rule 11; a release is above any pre-release of the same numbers; build metadata is dropped entirely.

A ^ or ~ range without a pre-release accepts pre-release versions (satisfies('1.2.3-beta', '^1.2.3') and satisfies('1.2.4-beta', '^1.2.3') are true; npm says false). A ^ or ~ range with a pre-release rejects every release version (satisfies('1.2.3', '^1.2.3-beta') and satisfies('1.2.4', '^1.2.3-beta') are false; npm says true).
^ and ~ look only at the first three segments, so satisfies('1.2.3.4', '~1.2.3.5') is true; operator comparators still compare four segments.

A hyphen range uses JS split(' - ', 2), which drops everything after the second piece: '1.0.0 - 2.0.0 - 3.0.0' means >=1.0.0 <=2.0.0. Partial upper bounds are not expanded (1.0 - 2 means <=2, npm means <3.0.0).

Range cleanup uses ECMAScript \s (includes U+00A0, U+FEFF, U+2028) after operators and in the 2+ run collapse, String.prototype.trim (strips U+FEFF), and splits only on ASCII space. Rust's \s and str::trim do not treat U+FEFF as whitespace, and a split on char::is_whitespace would also split on tabs and newlines.

'||' alternatives are evaluated left to right and stop at the first true; space-separated comparators stop at the first false. A malformed comparator after the deciding one is never parsed and raises no error ('1.0.0 || foo' is true for 1.0.0 and throws for 2.0.0).

Errors are JS built-ins: TypeError for wrong argument or operator types, Error for invalid versions and operators. Tests match the message text, and every fixture records the exact message (the invalid-version message embeds the raw input, unescaped, including quotes and newlines).
The invalid-operator message lists the operators as Object.keys(operatorResMap).join('|'), insertion order: >|>=|=|<=|<|!=.
The operator TypeError names the JS typeof of the operator: undefined, object (also for null and arrays), boolean, number (also NaN), bigint, function.

compare checks the operator type, then the operator value, then v1, then v2; compareVersions parses v1 completely before looking at v2. Which error appears for inputs with several problems depends on this order.

All five functions accept any JS value at run time: validate and validateStrict return false, compareVersions and compare throw TypeError, satisfies throws from the library or from the runtime. A Rust API taking &str cannot receive these; every such case has 'nonstring' in its name (48 cases) so the strategy can cover them with one divergence glob (*nonstring*) or a Value-taking binding.

satisfies with a non-string range fails inside String.prototype.replace lookup, so the message is V8's (Node 24.18): 'range.replace is not a function', "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'replace')". These four cases carry ignore-message.

test/sort.ts sorts with Array.prototype.sort(compareVersions), which is stable (ES2019+); ties such as '1.0' and '1.0.0' keep input order. Fixtures record every ordered pair of each sort test's input; a stable sort over those results reproduces the expected order (checked when recording).

free: Module layout and helper names (tryParse, forceType, isWildcard, compareStrings, operatorResMap, allowedOperators, assertValidOperator).
How a version is represented after parsing (the source uses RegExpMatchArray with undefined holes).
Whether the regexes are regexes at all, as long as the accepted language is identical (including the leaks above).
The Rust error type's shape (one enum with variants, or several types), as long as error-map.json maps the source categories and Display reproduces the message text.
The Rust type for the operator (string or an enum with FromStr), as long as the invalid-operator cases are covered by fixtures or a recorded divergence.
compareVersions' Rust return type (i32 or Ordering), as long as the binding serializes -1, 0 and 1.
Performance and regex engine complexity (the source regexes backtrack; nothing observable depends on it within the 10 s case timeout).
JS packaging: ESM and UMD builds, the browser global, source maps and .d.ts files.
